📦 Offline LLM Knowledge System - Your Docs. Their Browser. Zero Internet.
No API keys. No servers. No internet. Just a zip file.
Status: Open Source · github.com/muthuishere/offline-llm-knowledge-system
The Problem
You’re deploying software to a factory floor. An aircraft carrier. A hospital network. A customer site behind a firewall.
Your team needs an AI assistant that knows your product. Your runbooks. Your debug commands. But there’s no internet.
You can’t call OpenAI. You can’t hit Anthropic. You can’t even reach HuggingFace.
You have a browser. That’s it.
This isn’t niche. Every enterprise, every OT network, every air-gapped system hits this wall.
What I Built
Two web applications. Both run in the browser. Zero backend.
App 1: Export (needs internet once)
•
Drop your documents
•
Choose your LLM (Phi-3-mini, Gemma-2B, or TinyLlama)
•
Model downloads from HuggingFace
•
Documents get chunked and embedded
•
Click Export → one zip file (500MB–2.4GB)
App 2: Import (never needs internet)
•
Drop the zip
•
Chat immediately
•
All answers from your docs
No Python. No Node. No Docker. Just modern browsers.
One zip. One import. Chat works - forever offline.
The Use Cases
Why Browsers?
Because a browser is already there. Always No installer. No admin rights. No dependency hell. No pip install. No PATH drama.
A tiny model runs entirely on CPU in WebAssembly. No GPU needed.
The entire stack runs inside one browser tab.
What’s in the zip
knowledge-base.zip ├── manifest.json ← model config, chunk settings, source list ├── chunks.json ← all document chunks with pre-computed vectors ├── orama-index.json.gz ← BM25 full-text search index (offline) ├── instructions.md ← your system prompt ├── sources/ ← original documents ├── model/ ← LLM weights (Phi-3-mini, Gemma-2B, or TinyLlama) └── embed-cache/ ← embedding model (bge-small-en-v1.5, pre-bundled)
Everything the browser needs. Nothing more.
The search pipeline
When you ask a question:
1.
Your query → 384-dimensional vector (ONNX worker, off main thread)
2.
Hybrid search: BM25 text + cosine similarity → top 3 chunks
3.
Chunks injected into the user message (not system) → model grounds on them
4.
LLM generates answer in a Web Worker → UI stays responsive
5.
Answer streams back token by token
Runs entirely on CPU. Works anywhere.
Why context goes in the user turn, not system
Small models are trained on instruction-following. They attend much better to content in the user turn than buried in the system prompt.
Classic RAG mistake: stuff retrieved chunks into the system message. Models treat them as background noise, not grounding facts. Answers get vague. Hallucinations creep in.
Gemma-2B gives the best grounding accuracy among the three models I tested (Phi-3-mini, Gemma-2B, TinyLlama).
Correct shape for small models:
System: (tiny, stable, &lt;200 chars) "You are a grounded assistant. Answer only from context. If unsure, say so. Cite sources. Complete sentences."
User: Context: [DOC 1 - maintenance-guide.md] ... chunk text ...
[DOC 2 - error-codes.md] ... chunk text ...
Question: Why does error E-4417 appear after restart?
This shape gets 3–5× better grounding on smaller models than standard RAG prompts.
Why tiny chunks
Standard RAG uses 512-token chunks. For a 4K-context model running 3-chunk retrieval, that’s 1,536 tokens before you even add the question. Small models have no room left for output.
I use 100-token chunks (~400 chars).
Three chunks = 400 tokens. Plenty of room. More focused retrieval. Better answers.
The Stack
The embed model bundling trick
At export time, after embedding runs, I drain the browser’s transformers-cache Cache API - where transformers.js stores model files from HuggingFace.
I capture only the model files (not CDN runtime), bundle them as embed-cache/N.bin with a URL index.
At import time, the unzip worker restores them into cache with original URLs as keys.
When the embed worker starts pipeline(), transformers.js finds files in cache. Zero network requests.
Fully offline after one export.
What This Unlocks
•
No-internet deployments: factory floors, ships, aircraft, hospitals, government networks
•
Data sovereignty: your docs never leave your machine. Ever.
•
Zero infrastructure: no vector DB, no GPU server, no API keys
•
Portability: one zip, any browser, any OS
•
Customizable: swap the LLM, change the prompt, add docs - just re-export
•
Debuggable: kb.ask("question"), kb.search("question"), kb.prompt("question") in the console
The Console API
This tool is for technical environments. So there’s a full console API for testing without the UI:
// Ask a question (embed + search + LLM) await kb.ask("Why does error E-4417 appear after restart?")
// Just show what documents were retrieved await kb.search("network timeout configuration")
// Show the full prompt being sent to the LLM (debug) await kb.prompt("How do I restart the monitoring service?")
// Show conversation history kb.history()
// Batch test multiple questions await kb.batch([ "What is the default retry limit?", "How do I clear the event log?", "What ports need to be open?" ])
Drop this in your debug session. Keep it in your ops runbook. Test your knowledge base before shipping the zip to the field.
Why Now
The models got small enough.
TinyLlama: 550MB. Gemma-2B: 1.4GB. Phi-3-mini: 1.3GB.
The tooling matured: WebLLM, transformers.js, Orama.
WebAssembly made CPU inference practical.
Gemma-2B delivers the best accuracy while staying under 1.6GB.
The gap between “LLM works on your laptop” and “LLM works with your data in your browser” closed.
It’s now 15 lines of config and a zip file.
